newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon's Solidere to open share ownership.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon's Solidere to open share ownership.

text.p: Lebanon's biggest company Solidere said on Thursday it planned to lift all ownership restrictions on its shares and allow foreign investors and local institutions to buy them.
The changes would be made in October when the distribution of company shares to property owners in central Beirut was expected to be complete, Chairman Nasser Chammaa told Reuters.

"The board felt it will serve the best interests of the shareholders to open up investment in the shares of the company to institutional investors all over the world and to Lebanese banks and Lebanese companies which have been excluded," he said.

Chammaa said in an interview Solidere's directors had decided to call an extraordinary shareholders' meeting to approve proposals for lifting ownership restrictions. The decision would also need government approval.
The date of the meeting would be announced next week.

Shares in the $1.93 billion real estate company, flagship of Lebanon's postwar reconstruction, cannot currently be owned by non-Arabs. Lebanese banks and financial institutions and most local companies are also barred from ownership.

Solidere began rebuilding the war-ravaged centre of Beirut in 1994. Infrastructure work is due for completion in August 1998 and Solidere is already putting up new buildings and selling plots for development.
It calls the 1.8 million square metres project on the Mediterranean seafront the major urban redevelopment of the 1990s.
When the ownership changes are made, "there will be no restrictions on transferability except for the 10 percent limit on ownership of the company's shares by a single owner," Chammaa said.
He said there was an appetite for direct investment in Solidere among international institutional investors.
This was shown by the success of its GDRs (Global Depositary Receipts), which were trading on the London Stock Exchange well above the price of the underlying shares on the Beirut bourse.
Researches by international institutions also showed the shares were heavily undervalued and the GDRs still had room for upward movement, Chammaa said.
Robert Fleming Securities recently estimated the Net Asset Value per GDR at $25 compared with the price of $16-$17 in London and the $11.5 price of the shares in Beirut.

"It's a very good time to do it now," Chammaa said of the proposed changes. "We've already got a lot of international visibility from institutional investors, many of whom are interested in investing directly."

Lifting restrictions in October was planned to coincide with the completion of the distribution of 100 million A shares being awarded to property owners in central Beirut in exchange for their rights, Chammaa said.
Eleven million A shares remained to be distributed, he said.
"We wouldn't do this operation if the distribution process was not complete, because it's seen as putting downward pressure on the shares," he added.
He did not expect the changes to have a negative affect on the GDRs. Market sources expected the underlying shares to reach the GDR price level by the time the A shares distribution ended.
Solidere's GDR programme is limited to 6.7 million GDRs issued last November. Under the terms of a lockup on the GDRs no more can be issued until December 1998.
Chammaa said the ownership changes would have a positive impact on Lebanon's capital markets because foreigners who came to invest in Solidere would look for other shares on the market.
"Institutional investors like to set up a portfolio in a country, not just in one company," Chammaa said. "This will definitely be a big plus for the capital markets in Lebanon."
